stories.headline: Bihar MLC polls: Upper caste candidates dominate election results
stories.title: Bihar MLC polls: Upper caste candidates dominate election results
stories.summary: The Opposition Congress party which had put up its candidates on five seats has failed to win even a single seat in the elections
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'election results' in title weight 64
article_sentences: Out of eight State legislative Council seats which had gone to poll on October 23, 2026 and final results of them which were scheduled to be announced on October 27, some are new faces with upper caste dominating the poll on six seats while, the Backward caste and Extremely backward caste candidates won one seat each respectively from Kosi and Tirhut Graduate constituencies.

Out of eight seats, the upper-caste Bhumihar candidates won on five seats and one by a Rajput candidate while, the Other Backward (Yadav) and Extremely Backward Caste (mallah---boatmen/ Fishermen) candidates won on one seat each from Kosi and Tirhut Graduate constituencies.
The Opposition Congress party which had put up its candidates on five seats has failed to win even a single seat in the elections.

Five upper-caste Bhumihar candidates are Neeraj Kumar Singh (Patna Graduate), Sanjiv Kumar Singh (Patna Teachers), Suresh Rai (Darbhanga Teachers), Sarvesh Kumar (Darbhanga Graduate) and Narendra Singh (Tirhut Teachers).

Out of these five upper caste winning candidates, three Sarvesh Kumar (Darbhanga Graduate seat) and Narendra Singh (Tirhut Teachers seat), and from the other ruling coalition partner JD-U is Neeraj Kumar Singh from Patna Graduate seat are from ruling NDA bloc while, the other two from upper caste Bhumihar community are: Opposition Rashtriya Janata Dal Sanjiv Kumar from Patna Teachers seat and Jan Suraaj Party candidate Suresh Rai from Darbhanga Teachers seats.

One Independent candidate Rahul Raj from Saran Teachers constituency is from upper caste Rajput community while, Narendra Kumar Yadav from BJP from Kosi Graduate seat is from Other Backward Yadav (OBC) caste and the Extremely Backward Caste (EBC) candidate Vanshidhar Brajwasi is from mallah (boatman, Fishermen) community who won the poll from Tirhut Graduate seat as an Independent candidate.

Out of eight, the new faces are Sanjiv Kumar Singh from RJD, who won the Patna Teachers constituency, defeating the several-time MLC from the seat, Nawal Kishore Yadav from BJP, Suresh Rai from Jan Suraaj Party, who won from Darbhanga Teachers seat, defeating the veteran sitting Congress MLC Madan Mohan Jha, Rahul Raj, the Independent candidate from Saran Teachers constituency and the Tirhut Graduate constituency candidate Vanshidhar Brajwasi.

stories.headline: Reading the mountain before we build on it
stories.title: Reading the mountain before we build on it
stories.summary: Jammu and Kashmir is often described in poetry, but its mountains also speak in a language of numbers. One recent set of numbers deserves the attention of every planner, engineer, farmer and traveller who cares for this land. In August 2026, the journal Scientific Reports, part of Nature Portfolio, published a study on landslide risk in our region. The paper is titled GIS based multi criteria landslide susceptibility assessment in the northwestern Himalaya, Jammu and Kashmir, India. It was led by Prof Avtar Singh Jasrotia and researchers from the Department of Geology at the University of Jammu, and it appeared on August 28. The study mapped 42,950.43 square kilometres of mountainous terrain across Jammu and Kashmir. The researchers looked at slope, rock type, rainfall, rivers, land use and the distance of each place from roads, and then asked a simple question. Where is the ground most likely to give way? The answer was clear. About 28.08 per cent of the mapped area, or roughly 12,062 square kilometres, falls in the high or very high landslide susceptibility zones. In plain words, more than one fourth of the mapped land needs extra care before any digging or building begins. Proximity to roads was found among the important variables in the modelling, which means that slopes disturbed by road construction deserve special attention. It is important to read this finding in the right spirit. It does not say that roads are bad. A road is a lifeline in the mountains. It carries the patient to the hospital, the child to school and the apple to the market. The study only tells us that the hill has its own temperament, and that good planning works best when it begins with a good map. The same spirit was visible at the 13th Sustainable Mountain Development Summit, held at the Shalimar campus of SKUAST Kashmir on October 12, 2026. Chief Minister Omar Abdullah spoke there about making Jammu and Kashmir the first Himalayan region with a full Mountain Development Policy. The talk included scientific road building, safe waste handling at new tourist places and respect for the carrying limits of fragile slopes. A policy of this kind grows stronger when it rests on evidence, and the new landslide map offers exactly that. Many hands have been working on this subject. Last year, a study on landslides was completed with the contribution of engineers and assistant professors of Geology and Geography, and the writer was glad to be one of its authors. A related paper on landslide risk along the national highways of Jammu and Kashmir was presented at a conference in New Zealand on February 3 and 4, 2026. These are modest efforts, meant as one more brick in a wall of knowledge that many scholars are building together. Some years ago, the Environment Committee of the Legislative Council was headed by this writer. The committee met forest officers, universities and climate experts, including some from Hyderabad, and held awareness programmes at nearly a dozen district headquarters. A document for the region was prepared. Its recommendations did not turn into policy, and perhaps a little more energy from the chair would have helped. The lesson is a happy one all the same. Good reports are never wasted, and the new policy could begin by reading them afresh alongside the new landslide map. Weather adds urgency. Rain and snow are behaving differently now, and dry springs, cloudbursts and flash floods are becoming more common. Roads, tunnels, hotels and homes can all be checked against hazard maps before approval. A geological check before work, good drainage and safe dumping of soil will keep slopes steady and families safe. The economy of the region also has a stake in this. Horticulture earns about ₹10,000 crore every year, supports around 35 lakh people and adds about 6 to 7 per cent to the region’s GDP, according to the NITI Aayog roadmap. Land in Kashmir is limited, and once an orchard becomes concrete it does not come back. Compact towns and sensible tall buildings can save farmland, as long as water supply, sewage and earthquake safety are checked first. Tourism, too, can grow with the mountains and not against them. It feeds hoteliers, drivers, guides, artisans and pony handlers, and it deserves full support. New places beyond Gulmarg, Pahalgam and Sonamarg can share the benefits more widely. A place should be ready before guests arrive, with working sewage treatment, waste disposal, water and parking. A published study of how many visitors a place can comfortably take, reviewed from time to time, would be a big help. All these threads need one hand to hold them. Roads, forests, tourism, farming, towns and disaster management work best under a common plan. That plan can have clear targets, open data, a voice for villagers and farmers and a yearly report card that everyone can read. The choice before us is not between development and nature. It is between development that understands the mountain from the beginning and development that learns about it later. With the new policy, the new research and the goodwill of many institutions, Jammu and Kashmir has a fine chance to choose the first path. If it does, the results will show in stable slopes, green orchards, clean rivers and secure livelihoods. Caring for our mountains is not just a nice idea. It is a matter of safety, income and our future. Let us keep learning from the hills, and from each other. Dr S Bashir Ahmad Veeri is a serving legislator from South Kashmir and contributes occasionally on public policy and governance.

stories.headline: The 2026 Midterms
stories.title: The 2026 Midterms
stories.summary: What does democracy mean when a government’s decisions are felt far beyond its borders, in bombed neighbourhoods, displaced families, rising fuel prices and weakened international restraints on power? As Americans approach the 3 November 2026 midterm elections, this question reaches the heart of electoral accountability: will voters judge the Trump administration only by domestic prices and partisan loyalties, or also by the human consequences of American power abroad? A Pew Research Center survey published on 8 October found that 84 per cent of registered voters considered the economy very important to their vote; 73 per cent said the future of democracy mattered greatly, while 57 per cent named foreign policy. These priorities are intertwined. Military escalation can unsettle energy markets and household budgets, while spending choices determine what governments fund at home and abroad. The question is whether voters will connect these consequences, or debate each in isolation. Iran is the most immediate test. The conflict, which began with US and Israeli strikes in February, has become a strategic gamble and a domestic political liability. Pew’s survey of September 28–October 4 found that 65 per cent of Americans disapproved of President Donald Trump’s handling of US military action against Iran, while 33 per cent approved. Only 16 per cent were very or extremely confident that the administration would achieve its goals; 77 per cent expected the conflict to last at least another six months. These figures raise questions about the war’s objectives, civilian protection, regional escalation and the absence of a credible political endgame. Reports that Trump would avoid attacking Iran before the midterms while negotiations continue sharpen the dilemma. If military decisions are adjusted around an electoral calendar, voters can ask whether strategy is being driven by long-term security or short-term political calculation. Iran’s government must also be scrutinised for its own conduct and regional actions; criticism of Washington does not require romanticising Tehran. But one state’s abuses do not remove the obligation to assess another state’s use of force under consistent standards: evidence, international law, civilian protection and a realistic path to de-escalation. Uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz affects oil prices, shipping and insurance, transmitting geopolitical risk into household budgets worldwide. A president cannot credibly promise economic stability while treating the consequences of military action as incidental. Voters should ask what measurable outcome would count as success, what the exit strategy is, and who will bear the costs if the conflict expands. Human rights abroad and the question of American consent Iran is only one part of the larger moral and political question. US support for Israel amid the devastation in Gaza, violence in Lebanon, and coercive rhetoric towards other territories raise questions about how consistently Washington applies its stated commitment to human rights. The issue is whether officials investigate credible evidence of civilian harm, scrutinise allies as well as adversaries, and make military assistance conditional on compliance with law. Human rights should not be a vocabulary deployed against geopolitical rivals and abandoned when an ally is involved. Civilian deaths, forced displacement, restrictions on humanitarian access, arbitrary detention and allegations of collective punishment require serious, independent examination wherever they occur. The same standard should apply to US policy, including the foreseeable consequences of arms transfers, sanctions, military operations and security partnerships. Where legal findings remain contested or facts incomplete, analysis must say so. Uncertainty is not a reason for silence, but neither is it a licence to present allegations as adjudicated facts. At home, immigration enforcement, detention and deportation practices have prompted concerns about due process, family separation and the treatment of vulnerable people. Governments may enforce borders and pursue security objectives; they remain bound by constitutional protections and legal obligations. The key questions are whether safeguards work, whether allegations of abuse are independently investigated, and whether affected people have meaningful access to remedies. It would be revealing to discover whether American voters approve or disapprove of human rights violations attributed to the Trump administration—or regard them as secondary to economic interests, immigration control or national security. Existing polling indicates broad disapproval of Trump’s handling of Iran, but it does not establish whether voters would punish the administration electorally for civilian harm, due-process violations or the conduct of US-backed forces. A rigorous poll would ask about specific actions, distinguish verified findings from allegations, and test whether attitudes change when respondents learn about civilian consequences and legal obligations. It would examine partisan differences without assuming party identity determines every moral judgment. The answers could reveal whether human rights function as a genuine democratic standard or are invoked selectively to reinforce prior loyalties. Political theory helps frame the issue. Robert Dahl’s account of polyarchy emphasises meaningful competition and opportunities to contest power; Jürgen Habermas’s public sphere depends on access to information and open debate. Elections confer authority, but they cannot make that authority a blank cheque. A vote for a party cannot be read as approval of every action by its leaders. Those actions must remain open to scrutiny between elections as well as during them. Beyond November: Accountability, not just party victory The midterms will be counted in seats, margins and turnout. Their deeper meaning will depend on whether Congress can investigate executive decisions, scrutinise military spending, demand legal justifications and make oversight more than partisan theatre. The test is whether institutions apply consistent standards regardless of who occupies the White House. The economy remains central. Pew found that 84 per cent of registered voters ranked it as very important to their midterm vote, while foreign policy mattered to 57 per cent. The Iran conflict may influence voters partly through petrol prices and economic insecurity. opening: What does democracy mean when a government’s decisions are felt far beyond its borders, in bombed neighbourhoods, displaced families, rising fuel prices and weakened international restraints on power?

As Americans approach the 3 November 2026 midterm elections, this question reaches the heart of electoral accountability: will voters judge the Trump administration only by domestic prices and partisan loyalties, or also by the human consequences of American power abroad?
body: A Pew Research Center survey published on 8 October found that 84 per cent of registered voters considered the economy very important to their vote; 73 per cent said the future of democracy mattered greatly, while 57 per cent named foreign policy.
These priorities are intertwined.
Military escalation can unsettle energy markets and household budgets, while spending choices determine what governments fund at home and abroad.
The question is whether voters will connect these consequences, or debate each in isolation.
Iran is the most immediate test.
The conflict, which began with US and Israeli strikes in February, has become a strategic gamble and a domestic political liability.
Pew’s survey of September 28–October 4 found that 65 per cent of Americans disapproved of President Donald Trump’s handling of US military action against Iran, while 33 per cent approved.
Only 16 per cent were very or extremely confident that the administration would achieve its goals; 77 per cent expected the conflict to last at least another six months.
These figures raise questions about the war’s objectives, civilian protection, regional escalation and the absence of a credible political endgame.
Reports that Trump would avoid attacking Iran before the midterms while negotiations continue sharpen the dilemma.
If military decisions are adjusted around an electoral calendar, voters can ask whether strategy is being driven by long-term security or short-term political calculation.
Iran’s government must also be scrutinised for its own conduct and regional actions; criticism of Washington does not require romanticising Tehran.

But one state’s abuses do not remove the obligation to assess another state’s use of force under consistent standards: evidence, international law, civilian protection and a realistic path to de-escalation.
Uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz affects oil prices, shipping and insurance, transmitting geopolitical risk into household budgets worldwide.
A president cannot credibly promise economic stability while treating the consequences of military action as incidental.
Voters should ask what measurable outcome would count as success, what the exit strategy is, and who will bear the costs if the conflict expands.
Human rights abroad and the question of American consent Iran is only one part of the larger moral and political question.

US support for Israel amid the devastation in Gaza, violence in Lebanon, and coercive rhetoric towards other territories raise questions about how consistently Washington applies its stated commitment to human rights.
The issue is whether officials investigate credible evidence of civilian harm, scrutinise allies as well as adversaries, and make military assistance conditional on compliance with law.
Human rights should not be a vocabulary deployed against geopolitical rivals and abandoned when an ally is involved.
Civilian deaths, forced displacement, restrictions on humanitarian access, arbitrary detention and allegations of collective punishment require serious, independent examination wherever they occur.
The same standard should apply to US policy, including the foreseeable consequences of arms transfers, sanctions, military operations and security partnerships.
Where legal findings remain contested or facts incomplete, analysis must say so.
Uncertainty is not a reason for silence, but neither is it a licence to present allegations as adjudicated facts.
At home, immigration enforcement, detention and deportation practices have prompted concerns about due process, family separation and the treatment of vulnerable people.
Governments may enforce borders and pursue security objectives; they remain bound by constitutional protections and legal obligations.
The key questions are whether safeguards work, whether allegations of abuse are independently investigated, and whether affected people have meaningful access to remedies.

It would be revealing to discover whether American voters approve or disapprove of human rights violations attributed to the Trump administration—or regard them as secondary to economic interests, immigration control or national security.

Existing polling indicates broad disapproval of Trump’s handling of Iran, but it does not establish whether voters would punish the administration electorally for civilian harm, due-process violations or the conduct of US-backed forces.

Elections confer authority, but they cannot make that authority a blank cheque.
A vote for a party cannot be read as approval of every action by its leaders.
Those actions must remain open to scrutiny between elections as well as during them.

stories.headline: Cooperative Federalism: The Constitutional Compact India Must Renew
stories.title: Cooperative Federalism: The Constitutional Compact India Must Renew
stories.summary: India’s federalism is not a contest over who commands and who complies. It is a constitutional compact designed to reconcile national unity with regional autonomy, common purpose with political diversity, and effective governance with democratic accountability. Its success depends not on the concentration of power in one centre, but on the capacity of the Union and the States to exercise their respective constitutional responsibilities in partnership. As India confronts increasingly complex economic, environmental, technological and geopolitical challenges, cooperative federalism has become more than a constitutional aspiration. It is an essential condition of democratic stability, institutional trust and effective government. The constitutional scholar Granville Austin captured this distinctive design in The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation, describing India’s model as one of “cooperative federalism.” His insight remains relevant: India’s federal structure was shaped by the need to preserve national unity while accommodating an extraordinary diversity of languages, cultures, political traditions and regional aspirations. The constitutional challenge was never simply to distribute power, but to make that distribution work. The constitutional architecture of cooperation The Constitution does not expressly use the phrase “cooperative federalism,” but its institutional architecture reflects that philosophy. Article 1 describes India as a “Union of States.” Articles 245 and 246, read with the Seventh Schedule, distribute legislative powers between the Union and the States. Articles 256 and 257 address aspects of executive coordination, while Articles 268 to 293 govern financial relations. Article 263 provides for an Inter-State Council, and Article 280 establishes the Finance Commission. These provisions establish both the autonomy of constitutional authorities and the need for coordination. They do not envisage government as a collection of watertight compartments. The Constitution also gives the Union significant powers, reflecting the historical circumstances of Partition and the imperative of national integration. Yet this central strength must not be confused with an unrestricted authority to displace State autonomy. The constitutional framework requires a balance between national interests and the legitimate responsibilities of elected State governments. The Supreme Court’s decision in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) reinforced the constitutional significance of federalism, while the Court’s wider jurisprudence has emphasised that constitutional powers must be exercised within their prescribed limits. Federalism is therefore not merely an administrative arrangement. It is part of the constitutional structure through which democracy is organised, and power is held accountable. A strong Union requires strong States The false choice between a strong Union and strong States must be rejected. National unity is not weakened when States exercise legitimate autonomy; it is strengthened when regional aspirations find democratic expression within the constitutional framework. India’s federal experiment differs from federations formed through an agreement among previously sovereign political units. Its Constitution sought to preserve the unity of an exceptionally diverse country while assigning substantial responsibilities to different levels of government. That design requires flexibility, consultation and mutual respect. States are not administrative branches of the Union. They possess constitutionally defined powers and independent democratic mandates. Equally, State autonomy does not extinguish the Union’s responsibility for national security, macroeconomic stability and matters constitutionally entrusted to it. The objective must be constitutional partnership, not institutional rivalry. Political diversity must not become federal discrimination India’s democratic landscape is marked by different political parties governing at the Centre and across the States. This is neither an anomaly nor a constitutional inconvenience. It is a natural expression of electoral pluralism. The Constitution recognises governments formed through democratic processes, not governments entitled to cooperation only when their political affiliations coincide. A State government cannot be treated as an adversary merely because it belongs to the Opposition. Nor should legitimate access to national resources, institutional consultation or development opportunities depend on political alignment. The true test of cooperative federalism arises when governments disagree. Constitutional maturity lies in managing differences through dialogue, established institutions and law—not through confrontation, public recrimination or the politicisation of constitutional offices. Governments change; the federal compact must endure. Fiscal federalism: Autonomy requires resources The most consequential test of federalism is financial. States deliver many of the public services citizens experience directly, including healthcare, education, policing, agriculture, welfare and local infrastructure. Yet their ability to discharge these responsibilities depends substantially on the distribution of taxation powers, transfers and grants. A federation cannot function equitably if responsibilities are decentralised while financial discretion is disproportionately centralised. The Finance Commission is therefore a pivotal constitutional institution. Tax devolution and grants-in-aid must be guided by transparent principles that reconcile the needs of less-developed States, population-related responsibilities, fiscal discipline and developmental performance. States also require sufficient fiscal space to respond to local priorities and innovate in public policy. Predictable transfers, timely payments and meaningful consultation are essential to that autonomy. Fiscal federalism should not become a relationship between a permanent donor and a dependent recipient. It must recognise the States as partners in generating national prosperity and delivering constitutional promises. The GST Council: Cooperation without compulsory unanimity The Goods and Services Tax Council, established under Article 279A, offers an important institutional example. It brings the Union and the States into a common forum to deliberate on significant questions of indirect taxation and the functioning of the GST system. The experience has also exposed tensions over revenue compensation, fiscal autonomy, tax rates and the balance between uniformity and State flexibility. These disagreements do not necessarily indicate failure. Federal systems are designed to accommodate competing interests. The real test is whether institutional mechanisms permit disagreements to be negotiated fairly. The GST Council’s enduring lesson is that cooperation does not require unanimity on every question. It requires a genuine commitment to consultation, reasoned compromise and shared responsibility. Governors and the limits of constitutional discretion The office of the Governor presents another important test of federal balance. The Governor occupies a constitutional position within the parliamentary system, but the democratic legitimacy of State government ordinarily derives from its elected legislature and its majority in the Assembly. Questions concerning assent to Bills, government formation and the exercise of discretionary powers must be resolved through constitutional principles rather than partisan calculations. In State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to the Governor of Punjab (2023), the Supreme Court underscored the importance of constitutional responsibility and the limits on gubernatorial inaction. The broader principle is that constitutional authorities must not frustrate the functioning of elected institutions through indefinite delay or an expansive interpretation of their discretion. The Governor is not an alternative political executive. The office must be exercised with restraint, neutrality and fidelity to the Constitution. Cooperative federalism requires every constitutional authority to respect the sphere of responsibility assigned to others. Cooperation for challenges that cross borders Competitive federalism has encouraged States to attract investment, improve infrastructure, generate employment and experiment with development strategies. Such competition can stimulate innovation and improve governance. But competition cannot substitute for cooperation where challenges transcend territorial boundaries. Air pollution moves across State borders. Rivers connect multiple jurisdictions. Migration, epidemics, energy security and transport infrastructure demand coordinated responses. Climate change, artificial intelligence and disaster management require shared standards, information and institutional capacity. India must therefore embrace competitive and cooperative federalism together: competition where it encourages better governance, and cooperation where common interests demand collective action. The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated how closely national coordination and State-level implementation are connected. It also exposed the costs of inadequate consultation and uneven institutional capacity. The lesson extends to future public health emergencies, environmental crises and technological disruptions. Renewing the institutions of federal dialogue India already possesses institutions capable of strengthening this partnership, but their effectiveness depends on regular engagement and political will. The Inter-State Council under Article 263 should be used more consistently for structured discussion of Centre-State relations and inter-State disputes. The Finance Commission must retain its credibility as an impartial constitutional institution. The GST Council should remain a forum for meaningful negotiation, and NITI Aayog should facilitate substantive policy cooperation rather than merely communicate decisions already taken. Parliament, too, must give serious consideration to State perspectives when legislative proposals substantially affect their constitutional responsibilities. Consultation must occur early enough to influence policy. It cannot be reduced to a procedural formality after decisions have effectively been made. Constitutional morality and the road ahead Ultimately, cooperative federalism depends as much on constitutional morality as on institutional design. The Union must respect legitimate State autonomy; States must recognise legitimate national interests; Governors must act impartially; and elected governments must exercise their powers responsibly. Political parties must distinguish the interests of the Republic from the immediate advantages of partisan competition. The gravest threat to federalism is not disagreement. It is the erosion of institutional trust through the politicisation of constitutional powers. India’s federal compact must now be renewed through transparent fiscal arrangements, predictable intergovernmental cooperation, stronger consultation and scrupulous respect for constitutional boundaries. The question is not whether the Union or the States should prevail. It is whether both can discharge their responsibilities more effectively by working together. A confident India must be a confident Union of confident States. As Granville Austin’s understanding of cooperative federalism reminds us, national unity and regional autonomy need not be competing objectives. Properly balanced, they reinforce each other. Cooperative federalism is not a concession from the Union to the States. It is a constitutional obligation arising from the structure of the Republic. Renewing that compact is essential to India’s democratic credibility, developmental ambitions and constitutional future. (The Author is a Senior Advocate, Supreme Court of India, a public intellectual and a constitutional expert)

stories.headline: Cabinet approves 3% hike in DA for Central Govt employees, pensioners
stories.title: Cabinet approves 3% hike in DA for Central Govt employees, pensioners
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 28: The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on Wednesday approved a 3 percent increase in Dearness Allowance (DA) for central government employees and Dearness Relief (DR) for pensioners, effective July 1, 2026. The increase will raise DA and DR from the existing 60 percent to 63 percent of basic pay and pension, to compensate for the impact of rising prices. The decision will benefit around 48.54 lakh central government employees and 68.71 lakh pensioners. The combined annual financial impact on the exchequer will be Rs 10,016.10 crore. The increase is in accordance with the accepted formula based on the recommendations of the 7th Central Pay Commission.

stories.headline: India votes against US embargo on Cuba at UN, urges end to unilateral sanctions
stories.title: India votes against US embargo on Cuba at UN, urges end to unilateral sanctions
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: India highlighted the severe humanitarian toll of the sanctions, including acute shortages of medicines and food, and called for dialogue, diplomacy, and the swift lifting of the embargo to support Cuba's development.

New York: India has reiterated its opposition to legislation that "adversely affects the sovereignty" of other states while backing a United Nations General Assembly resolution calling for an end to the long-running US economic embargo against Cuba.

Addressing the Assembly ahead of the ballot, Soumya Nair, a counsellor at India’s Permanent Mission to the UN, stated that New Delhi supports the global body's call urging member states to reject “laws and regulations with extraterritorial effects that adversely affect the sovereignty of other states and the progress and prosperity of their peoples”.

She stressed, “India reiterates the Assembly’s call to all states to refrain from promulgating and applying, and to repeal and invalidate such laws and measures in conformity with their obligations under the Charter of the United Nations and International Law”.
The resolution was adopted with 130 votes in favour, 17 against, and 25 abstentions.

The vote occurred following a tense confrontation on the Assembly floor on Tuesday, during which Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla approached the lectern to challenge US Permanent Representative Mike Waltz mid-address.
In response to the disruption, Assembly President Khalilur Rahman briefly halted proceedings to restore order.

Diplomatic friction escalated further on Wednesday when the United States expelled Richard Tur de la Concepción, First Secretary at the Cuban mission, following allegations that he physically confronted an American diplomat during Tuesday's incident, according to Ambassador Waltz.

Asserting a strict posture, Waltz declared, “If you lay a hand on an American diplomat in this body, there will be consequences,” adding, “That so-called diplomat today will be put on a plane back to Havana.”
The initial altercation occurred while Waltz was speaking to the General Assembly regarding alleged corruption within Cuba’s ruling leadership.

Commenting on the event, Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for UN Secretary-General António Guterres, criticised the breach of protocol during a Wednesday news briefing, stating, “We expect every delegation to respect the decorum of the General Assembly’s hall and to respect the rules and procedures of the General Assembly.”
He added that UN Safety and Security officers were deployed in larger numbers and “did a great job in ensuring that the situation did not get out of hand”.

Asserting a strict posture, Waltz declared, “If you lay a hand on an American diplomat in this body, there will be consequences,” adding, “That so-called diplomat today will be put on a plane back to Havana.” The initial altercation occurred while Waltz was speaking to the General Assembly regarding alleged corruption within Cuba’s ruling leadership.

Commenting on the event, Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for UN Secretary-General António Guterres, criticised the breach of protocol during a Wednesday news briefing, stating, “We expect every delegation to respect the decorum of the General Assembly’s hall and to respect the rules and procedures of the General Assembly.” He added that UN Safety and Security officers were deployed in larger numbers and “did a great job in ensuring that the situation did not get out of hand”.
